pharm: Fungistatic antibiotic derived from Penicillium that binds fungal microtubular proteins, disrupting mitosis, and deposits in keratin precursor cells so newly formed keratin resists dermatophyte invasion.
quick: 0.5 g daily (microsize); up to 0.75-1 g/day for widespread disease
Take with a fatty meal (e.g., milk) to greatly improve absorption
Excretion in milk unknown; weigh benefit vs. risk (animal tumorigenicity)
Monitor renal function on prolonged therapy; no defined adjustment
Contraindicated in hepatocellular failure; monitor LFTs
Periodic CBC, LFTs, renal function on prolonged use
summary: Griseofulvin is an oral fungistatic antibiotic used for dermatophyte infections of the skin, hair, and nails that are not adequately treated topically. Absorption is markedly improved when taken with a high-fat meal. It is contraindicated in pregnancy (Category X), porphyria, and hepatocellular failure, and carries risks of severe skin reactions, hepatotoxicity, and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol. It reduces the efficacy of warfarin and oral contraceptives. Therapy must continue until the organism is eradicated (weeks for skin; 4-6+ months for nails).
indications: Tinea unguium (onychomycosis) caused by susceptible dermatophytes (Epidermophyton, Microsporum, Trichophyton species)
Reserved for dermatophyte infections not adequately treated by topical therapy; not for trivial infections responsive to topical agents alone

dosage.d: 0.5 g daily (125 mg q.i.d., 250 mg b.i.d., or 500 mg once daily)
dosage.t: With a high-fat meal; continue until organism eradicated

dosage.d: Starting dose 0.75 g to 1 g/day, reduced gradually to 0.5 g or less after response
10 mg/kg/day in divided doses (30-50 lb: 125-250 mg/day; >50 lb: 250-500 mg/day)
dosage.n: Safety not established at >10 mg/kg/day or in children <=2 years

dosage.d: Tinea capitis 4-6 wk; tinea corporis 2-4 wk; tinea pedis 4-8 wk; fingernails >=4 mo; toenails >=6 mo
dosage.n: Relapse occurs if stopped before eradication

admin: Take with a high-fat meal (e.g., milk) - this can increase serum levels several-fold
Confirm diagnosis with KOH prep, fungal culture, or nail biopsy before starting
Continue therapy without interruption until the infecting organism is eradicated by clinical or lab confirmation
Concomitant topical antifungal therapy is usually required, particularly for tinea pedis
Observe general hygiene measures to control sources of infection or reinfection
moa: Griseofulvin is a fungistatic antibiotic that binds to fungal microtubular proteins (tubulin), interfering with spindle and cytoplasmic microtubule function and thereby inhibiting fungal mitosis. After oral absorption it is deposited in keratin precursor cells and has a greater affinity for diseased tissue; it binds tightly to newly formed keratin, which becomes resistant to fungal invasion. It is active against dermatophytes (Epidermophyton, Microsporum, Trichophyton) but has no effect on bacteria or other genera of fungi.

absolute: Pregnancy (Category X) - fetal harm; conjoined twins reported with first-trimester use
relative: History of penicillin sensitivity (possible cross-sensitivity, though penicillin-sensitive patients generally treated without difficulty)
Concomitant warfarin or estrogen-containing contraceptives (reduced efficacy)
monitor: Periodic renal, hepatic, and hematopoietic function on prolonged therapy
Signs of severe skin reaction (SJS/TEN, erythema multiforme)

preg: Contraindicated (Pregnancy Category X). Griseofulvin may cause fetal harm; two cases of conjoined twins were reported with first-trimester exposure, and it is embryotoxic and teratogenic in animals. It is contraindicated in women who are or may become pregnant during treatment. Estrogen-containing oral contraceptives may be less effective, so an alternate or additional form of birth control is advised. Male patients should wait at least 6 months after completing therapy before fathering a child.
lact: It is not known whether griseofulvin is excreted in human milk. Because many drugs are excreted in milk and because of tumorigenicity demonstrated in animal studies, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: Periodic monitoring of renal function is recommended during prolonged therapy. Proteinuria and nephrosis (sometimes associated with existing SLE) have been reported rarely. No specific dose adjustment is defined in the label.
hepatic: Contraindicated in hepatocellular failure. Elevations of AST, ALT, and bilirubin, jaundice, and hepatitis have been reported; monitor for hepatic adverse events and discontinue if warranted. Liver tumors occurred in mice with chronic high-dose feeding.

major: Warfarin-type anticoagulants (griseofulvin decreases anticoagulant activity; monitor INR and adjust dose during and after therapy)
Estrogen-containing oral contraceptives (reduced contraceptive efficacy and menstrual irregularities; use alternate/second method)
moderate: Cyclosporine (levels may be reduced, decreasing its effect)
Barbiturates (depress griseofulvin levels/activity; may need griseofulvin dose adjustment)
minor: Salicylates (serum salicylate concentrations may be decreased)
interactions.food: Take with a high-fat meal (e.g., milk) - significantly increases absorption and serum levels.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol. A disulfiram-like reaction (nausea, vomiting, flushing, tachycardia, severe hypotension) has been reported with alcohol ingestion during therapy.

monitoring: Clinical/laboratory confirmation of organism eradication (KOH, culture)
Watch for severe skin reactions and signs of photosensitivity
counsel: Take with a fatty meal or milk to help the drug work
Avoid alcohol - it can cause flushing, fast heartbeat, and a drop in blood pressure
Avoid intense or prolonged sunlight; use sun protection (photosensitivity)
Use an additional or alternate method of birth control - this drug can make oral contraceptives less effective and must not be used in pregnancy
Keep taking the full course even after symptoms improve; nail infections may take 4-6 months or more
Report rash, blistering, yellowing of skin/eyes, or numbness/tingling promptly
pk: Gradual; deposited in keratin, clinical response over weeks
Serum peak ~4 hours after a 0.5 g microsize dose (fasting)
Skin/keratin levels persist after plasma levels fall once discontinued
pearls: Absorption is erratic; always give with a high-fat meal (milk increased pediatric peak levels ~4-fold)
Reduces effectiveness of warfarin and estrogen-containing oral contraceptives
Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol - counsel abstinence
Pregnancy Category X; men should wait >=6 months after therapy before fathering a child
Continue until eradication confirmed - nails require months of treatment
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered with food. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose; do not double up. Consistent dosing is important to eradicate the infection.
overdose: Experience with overdose is limited. In case of overdosage, discontinue the medication, treat symptomatically, and institute supportive measures as required.
